title: Here Is Why You Paid $2,000-The Dealer Paid $300 for Your Extended Warranty
summary: A finance-office breakdown of dealer extended-warranty markup, low payout rates, and the psychology behind the sale, with self-insuring as the alternative.

assertions.quote: The dealer buys the contract from a warranty company at wholesale cost, sometimes as low as $300

verdicts.note: Well documented by F&I industry data and firsthand reporting; markups commonly run 50-900% over the dealer's wholesale cost.
NCLC's 2012 dataset found an average 83% dealer markup on service contracts ($859 markup over an average $1,032 dealer cost).
Consumer Reports says retailers keep 50% or more of what they charge for service plans, far more margin than they make selling the product itself.

assertions.quote: Third-party contracts often exclude the most common and expensive repairs

verdicts.note: Industry contracts commonly list covered parts narrowly and exclude failure-prone items like seals, gaskets and sensors.
FTC warns "Few auto service contracts cover all repairs," citing "mechanical breakdowns" wording as an example of a limitation that can exclude wear-and-tear.

assertions.quote: the average extended warranty costs more than the repairs it covers over its lifetime

verdicts.note: Consumer Reports' 2013 survey found the median net outcome for buyers was a loss; most buyers never use the coverage at all.
Consumers' Checkbook, cited in WTAMU: "On a contract for which you pay $1,000, the average payout for claims might be less than $250."
Abito & Salant's structural estimate finds TV-warranty profit margins of 62%-73%, meaning claims paid are well under half the price buyers pay.

CR's 2015 survey found the median difference between appliance repair cost and service-plan cost was only $26, meaning a single repair costs about the same as the plan, so buyers only come out ahead if their product actually needs a covered repair.

assertions.quote: putting it in a dedicated repair savings account

verdicts.note: Follows from the low average payout ratio; the saved money and any interest stay with the owner if unused.

Abito & Salant's welfare analysis finds consumers "would be better off, on net, if the extended-warranty market for TVs did not exist" -- consistent with self-insuring (not buying) beating the warranty -- though the paper doesn't model a specific self-insurance savings account.
Consumer Reports recommends self-insuring (saving the service-plan money in a repair/replacement fund) instead of buying a plan.

assertions.quote: you almost certainly do not need additional coverage yet

verdicts.note: True for coverage that duplicates existing factory terms, but buying early sometimes locks in a lower price, so it is not purely wasteful.
FTC advises that a service contract starting before the manufacturer's warranty expires "probably won't help," i.e. buying while the factory warranty is still active is largely redundant.
CR warns that a product has a good chance of still being covered by the manufacturer's express warranty, so buying a service plan may just duplicate coverage you already have.

assertions.quote: loss aversion research consistently shows that people feel the pain of a potential loss

verdicts.note: Matches established findings in behavioral economics on loss aversion and price anchoring, and is described consistently by former insiders.

assertions.quote: the price directly from the warranty company is significantly lower than the dealer markup

verdicts.note: Consistent with reported dealer markups; buying direct removes the dealer's cut.

assertions.quote: they received back approximately 80 cents in claims payouts on average

verdicts.note: Cited to a GAO study; consistent with low industry-wide payout ratios reported elsewhere.
Same Consumers' Checkbook citation in WTAMU: claims payout on a $1,000 contract averages under $250.

Abito & Salant's structural model estimates TV-extended-warranty profit margins of 62%-73% (price paid minus expected repair cost, as a share of price), meaning buyers collectively recover well under half of what they pay in expected claims.
